1.hook: You are about to call a model. What is on the other end of that call, and what does each call cost you?
objectives: Explain autoregressive generation and temperature to someone who has never seen a model call
Count tokens for a prompt and convert them to dollars without looking anything up
Name the four layers people conflate — model, API, framework, application — and say which one a given bug lives in
1.needs: Nothing. This is the first chapter — a working Python environment is all you need.

2.hook: The model gave you JSON. Twice. The third time it gave you JSON wrapped in an apology. How do you build on that?
objectives: Choose between prompting, function-calling and constrained decoding for a given reliability requirement
Design a schema whose field order improves the answer, and add an evidence quote that makes hallucination checkable
Size a concurrency limit from a rate limit, and distinguish the two controls people conflate
2.needs: Day 1 — what a model call is, tokens, the four layers.

3.hook: A user asks “what do I get charged for sitting at the dock?” Your policy document says “detention accrues at $65/hr.” Zero shared words. How do you find it?
objectives: Describe what an embedding is and what it is not, without saying “it captures semantic meaning”
Compute cosine and Euclidean distance by hand and state the relationship between them for unit vectors
Predict which of two retrieval failures is topical and which is propositional, and choose a chunking strategy on that basis
3.needs: Day 1 (tokens, cost) and Day 2 (structured output). Bring pen and paper — §3 has real arithmetic.

4.hook: Retrieval found the right paragraph. The answer is still wrong, and it cites a page that does not say what the answer claims. Which clause of the contract broke?
objectives: State the four-clause RAG contract and identify which clause a given failure violates
Compute retrieval recall on a golden set and explain why it is the ceiling on answer quality
Assemble a prompt with deliberate ordering, k, and citation grade rather than by default
4.needs: Day 3 — embeddings, distance, chunking. You will use the index you built.

5.hook: Your system is better than last week. Prove it. Not with a demo — with a number, and an interval around that number.
objectives: Build a golden set and explain why it, not the code, is the product
Read a retrieval metric and say what it hides — and why an aggregate score can rise while every user gets worse
Name the four biases of an LLM judge and calibrate one against human labels using Cohen's κ
5.needs: Day 4 — the RAG contract and a working pipeline to measure.

6.hook: Six days of parts. Today they become one system, and you argue for it in front of a room.
objectives: Trace Week 1 as a single causal chain and name what each day contributes to the final answer
Structure a demo as an argument in seven beats rather than a feature tour
Engineer a demo so a network failure or a slow model does not end it
6.needs: Days 1–5. This is a capstone day: the module is short and the build is long.

7.hook: The model does not call your function. It writes text that looks like a function call, and you decide what to do about it.
objectives: Write the agent loop in five steps from memory, without a framework
Choose termination conditions beyond max_steps and justify each one
Write a tool description that changes model behaviour, and explain why it is the highest-leverage prompt surface you control
7.needs: Day 2 (structured output) and Day 4 (prompt assembly). Week 2 begins here.

8.hook: “Which of our carriers had worse on-time performance than Ridgeline last quarter?” One retrieval cannot answer that. What can?
objectives: Match a query shape to the right pattern — routing, rewriting, decomposition, or correction
Compute reciprocal rank fusion by hand and explain why ranks beat scores
Price each pattern in tokens and latency, so you can say what agentic RAG costs before you propose it
8.needs: Day 7 (the agent loop) and Day 4 (the RAG contract).

9.hook: Five agents sound better than one. Count the tokens before you believe that.
objectives: Describe a worker agent as a tool whose implementation is another loop
Name the three failure modes — context loss, responsibility diffusion, cost explosion — and detect each in a trace
Argue the case against multi-agent for a given problem, with the token arithmetic to back it
9.needs: Days 7–8. Bring pen and paper — the token accounting is the argument.

10.hook: The model remembers nothing between calls. Everything that feels like memory is something you rebuilt and paid for again.
objectives: Distinguish the four memory types by what each is physically made of
Allocate a context window line by line as a budget, including the tool schemas people forget
Choose a compaction strategy and state precisely what it loses
10.needs: Days 7–9 — you need an agent whose context you can watch grow.

11.hook: Every tool you wrote works with your agent and nothing else. MCP is the answer to that, and it is smaller than it sounds.
objectives: Explain the N×M → N+M argument and where MCP sits in an architecture
Name the three primitives — tools, resources, prompts — and say who is in control of each
Define what a skill actually is, and avoid the stdio gotcha that breaks every first server
11.needs: Day 7 (tool calling). You will convert tools you already wrote.

12.hook: Every part passes its own test. The system still fails, and the failure lives in a seam nobody owns.
objectives: Name four problems that exist only at the seams between components
Evaluate a system end to end rather than part by part, and attribute latency and cost per node
Run an architecture review — a different format from a tutorial, with different rules
12.needs: Days 7–11. This is an integration day: the module is short and the build is long.

13.hook: Your hand-written golden set has forty cases and you have run out of imagination. Manufacture the rest.
objectives: Run four case generators — extractive, multi-hop, adversarial, persona — and state what each one tests
Calibrate a judge the way you would calibrate an instrument, including position bias as a measurement
Set a release gate above the noise floor, with a confidence interval you computed
13.needs: Day 5 (evals) and Day 12 (a working system). Bring pen and paper.

14.hook: Dense retrieval misses the shipment ID, the acronym, and the exact clause number. Everything in this chapter fixes one of those.
objectives: Map a retrieval failure to the specific tool that fixes it
Compute a BM25 score by hand and explain why its shape wins exactly where embeddings fail
Order the techniques — hybrid, fusion, rerank, contextual, dedupe — and know when to stop
14.needs: Days 3–4 and Day 13. Bring pen and paper — the BM25 and RRF arithmetic is the day.

15.hook: It works on your laptop, in a process you start by hand. Today other people's software calls it.
objectives: Name the four ways an LLM endpoint breaks normal API reflexes, and what each one forces
Design strictly nested timeouts including retries, and cancel work when the client disconnects
Build the three cache layers and calibrate a semantic-cache threshold yourself

16.hook: It failed at 3am and you were not there. What has to be in the trace for anyone to answer “why?” without you?
objectives: Say what a span must carry for an LLM failure, and why generic HTTP tracing under-determines it
Design a prompt-capture sampling policy you can afford, and version your config so “what changed Tuesday?” is answerable
Use the retrieval score distribution as a leading indicator of drift
16.needs: Day 15 (a served system). Bring pen and paper for the sampling arithmetic.

17.hook: “Can it run inside our VPC with no internet?” is not one question. It is three, and the answers change the architecture.
objectives: Choose among four deployment topologies by naming the constraint each one hits
Decompose the egress question into its three real questions and answer each
Produce the handover artifact set — the thing that makes you leavable
17.needs: Days 15–16. Bring pen and paper — the KV-cache and concurrency arithmetic changes architectures.

18.hook: Two questions you will answer in front of clients for the rest of your career: what does this cost at our volume, and can a document in our corpus attack us?
objectives: Order the cost levers by leverage and align a prompt so the cache actually hits
Compute a self-hosting break-even honestly, including the fixed costs that dominate at pilot scale
Treat indirect prompt injection as a trust boundary and name the residual risk that remains
18.needs: Days 15–17. Bring pen and paper — both calculations are the day.

19.hook: Week 4. The engineering is behind you. Now: how does the work get chosen, scoped, and defended?
objectives: Describe what a Forward Deployed Engineer actually is, and the four modes the role switches between
Run a discovery conversation across six areas without turning it into a requirements interview
Scope eval-first — the move that separates you from a vendor demo
19.needs: Weeks 1–3. This chapter is about the work around the work.

20.hook: Two days, one capstone. The constraint is not skill. It is deciding, out loud, what you are not shipping.
objectives: Cut a vertical slice and write the NOT SHIPPING list before you write code
Design the demo moment first and build backwards from it
Evaluate a whole document rather than a single answer, and fix failures in the right order
20.needs: Day 19 and everything before it. The module is short because the build is two days.

21.hook: A senior engineer at the client will try to take your system apart in a meeting. Make that a good meeting.
objectives: Define “defensible” concretely, and work a hardening checklist where every line has a reason
Answer the teardown question — what would you remove, and what would break
Write a case study whose limitations section is what makes it credible
21.needs: Day 20 — you need the capstone to defend.

22.hook: You know this material. That is precisely why you are about to teach it badly.
objectives: Explain why topic organisation is the wrong index for a lesson, and what the right one is
Build a lesson in eight beats, with an open loop that makes adults want the next one
Diagnose a wrong answer rather than merely marking it wrong
22.needs: Your LEARNING_LOG.md — your own confusions are the raw material for this chapter.

23.hook: Live, you cannot edit. Everything that makes live teaching survivable is decided before you start.
objectives: Work a pre-flight checklist and say why each line is on it
Recover on camera from a broken demo without losing the room
Handle the five question types, including the honest three-part “I don't know”
23.needs: Day 22 — you deliver the lesson you designed.

24.hook: The course ends today. What you do in the ninety days after it is what decides whether any of this held.
objectives: Give an eight-minute demo that lands without narration crutches
Build three portfolio surfaces that each do a different job
Write an honest gap assessment, pick two gaps, and replace this course's structure with a habit
24.needs: Everything. This is the last chapter.
